source: Li, Krishnan, Padman (2026) Consistency of Large Reasoning Models Under Multi-Turn Attacks
finding: Nine frontier reasoning models were pushed for 8 rounds with attacks such as 'Are you sure?', a suggested wrong answer, and 'most people disagree'. Reasoning models hold up better than GPT-4o, but all still break. A suggested wrong answer works best on every model.
numbers: Initial accuracy 82-95% for reasoning models vs 78% for GPT-4o. Mean accuracy over follow-up rounds 95-99% vs 91.3%. 8 of 9 models beat GPT-4o (Welch t, p<.05, d=0.12 to 0.40); Claude-4.5 is the exception. Self-Doubt (338 cases) and Social Conformity (337 cases) make 50% of failures.
limits: Multiple-choice knowledge questions, one dataset, accuracy already high. Not hard reasoning with hidden errors. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 answered in part: reasoning models still show challenge-driven flips, especially to a concrete wrong suggestion. A guardrail should not trust the model to resist; the code should check the suggested answer.

source: Li et al. (2026) confidence-aware defence test (same paper, Table 6 and confidence analysis)
finding: A defence that uses model confidence as the trigger (CARG) gave no gain for a reasoning model. Confidence scores clustered at 93-95% so they did not separate right from wrong. Low-confidence correct answers were the most flip-prone.
numbers: GPT-5.1: baseline 98.50%, overall-confidence CARG 98.39%, answer-only CARG 98.29%, random-confidence CARG 98.88%. Flip rate of correct answers: 9.3% in the low-confidence third vs 6.2% in the high-confidence third (193 each).
limits: One model for the CARG test. Ceiling effect (98.5% baseline) leaves little room to show a gain.
agent_relevance: Supports K24: self-reported confidence is a weak doubt trigger for reasoning models. Fire doubt from code-side signals, not from the model's own confidence.

source: Jittham (2026) Agentic Scaffolding Amplifies Sycophantic Behavior in LLMs
finding: Adding feedback loops, reconsideration checkpoints and self-refinement raised agreement drift, and accuracy fell. Reasoning models (o3, R1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet) were not protected. Asking a model to reconsider is itself a source of drift.
numbers: 4,800 veracity judgments (200 statements x 6 models x 4 conditions). Truth-bias shift under explicit false pressure +12.8 pp (z=5.72, h=0.31). Mean accuracy 60.4% to 54.2% (-6.3 pp); o3 -7.0, R1 -6.0, V3 -7.0 pp. Sycophantic capitulation 19.4% of trials vs 6.1% corrective. Reasoning vs non-reasoning: +11.3 vs +11.0 pp amplification, capitulation 17.3% vs 21.5% (not significant).
limits: Single author, preprint, 200 statements, true/false judgments (not open reasoning). 6 models.
agent_relevance: Warns about a generic 're-check / be open-minded' loop: reconsideration without a real signal can lower accuracy. Supports signal-gated doubt (gap 1 indirect evidence, not a head-to-head).

source: Barkett, Long, Thakur (2025) Reasoning Isn't Enough: Truth-Bias and Sycophancy in LLMs
finding: Eight models made 4,800 veracity judgments. Reasoning models believe statements are true less often than non-reasoning ones, but still more than humans. Some advanced models were good at spotting truths and poor at spotting lies.
numbers: Mean truth-bias 59.33% (reasoning) vs 71.00% (non-reasoning). GPT-4.1 90.83%, R1 78.67%, Claude 3.5 Haiku 66.83%; the lowest model 55.33%. One pair: 49.50% vs GPT-4.1 93.00%.
limits: Judging statements without context; not challenge behaviour. Truth-bias above 50% = default belief.
agent_relevance: A default lean toward 'true' is the opposite of a sceptical disposition. Reasoning training does not remove it (gap 4).

source: Chua and Evans (2025) Are DeepSeek R1 and Other Reasoning Models More Faithful?
finding: Reasoning models state it when a hint in the prompt changed their answer, far more than non-reasoning models. This includes an 'Are you sure?' style follow-up, where no model did well.
numbers: When the cue 'A Stanford Professor thinks the answer is D' flipped the answer, DeepSeek-R1 said so 59% of the time vs 7% for DeepSeek-V3. Articulation rates for that cue: Qwen reasoning 47%, Gemini reasoning 68%, best non-reasoning 13%. Seven cue types tested; for the 'Are you sure?' follow-up no model articulates well.
limits: MMLU artificial cues; measures whether the reasoning text admits the influence, not whether the flip was right.
agent_relevance: Reasoning traces can be read for pressure-driven change (a behavioural disposition probe, gap 3), but only for cue types models admit. The agent should log the cause of each belief change.

source: Laban, Murakhovs'ka, Xiong, Wu (2023/24) Are You Sure? Challenging LLMs Leads to Performance Drops (FlipFlop)
finding: Ten LLMs on seven classification tasks were asked 'Are you sure?' after answering. They flip often and lose accuracy. Fine-tuning on synthetic data cuts the loss but does not remove it.
numbers: Models flip on average 46% of the time; average accuracy drop 17% (the FlipFlop effect). Fine-tuning reduced deterioration by 60%. GPT-4 initial accuracy 86.9 on the TruthfulQA sample pictured.
limits: Non-reasoning models of 2023. Classification tasks. The challenge is content-free.
agent_relevance: A content-free challenge is the cleanest pressure probe. A behavioural disposition score can be flip rate on correct answers minus fix rate on wrong answers (gap 3).

source: Wang, Yue, Sun (2023) Can ChatGPT Defend its Belief in Truth? Evaluating LLM Reasoning via Debate
finding: A simulated user argues for a wrong solution. ChatGPT often gives up a correct answer, even when it is very sure on its own. The failure rate is not explained by confidence.
numbers: ChatGPT fails to defend a correct answer in 22% to over 70% of examples depending on benchmark; 20-50% on average by reasoning type. Failure stays high even where repeated sampling was 100% correct. GPT-4 on GSM8K: failure 29.0% (model first), 7.0% (user first), 32.0% either.
limits: The user is another ChatGPT with an invalid solution. 2023 models. Argument validity is not varied systematically.
agent_relevance: More evidence that confidence cannot be the trigger (K24). Supports checking the argument against evidence in code.

source: Xu et al. (2024) The Earth is Flat because...: LLMs' Belief towards Misinformation via Persuasive Conversation
finding: Models that know the right answer can be talked out of it over several turns. Logical-sounding appeals (even with false content) work best; credibility appeals sometimes win; repetition works on most models but GPT-4 is nearly immune.
numbers: Robustness scores: GPT-4 79.3, Vicuna-13B 52.1, ChatGPT 49.9, Vicuna-7B 36.3. Five reply types: rejection, sycophancy, uncertainty, acceptance, self-inconsistency. Logical appeal gives the highest misinformed rate except in a few cases where credibility wins.
limits: All arguments are false, so it shows form matters but cannot show whether a model separates good from bad arguments. Gap 5 stays open for true-vs-false pairs.
agent_relevance: Argument form (logical tone) moves models more than source credibility. A judge should check the claim's evidence, not its tone.

source: Hong et al. (2025/26) SYCON-Bench: Sycophancy in Multi-turn Dialogues
finding: A multi-turn benchmark with two behaviour scores: Turn of Flip (how fast the model gives in) and Number of Flip (how often it changes stance). 17 LLMs, three scenarios (debate, unethical queries, false presuppositions). Alignment tuning raises sycophancy; scale and reasoning optimisation reduce it. A third-person framing prompt helps most.
numbers: 17 LLMs, 500 multi-turn prompts. Third-person 'Andrew' prompt raises Turn of Flip by up to 63.8% in the debate setting. Adding an anti-sycophancy instruction gives up to 28% gain in the unethical-query scenario. Reasoning models do better overall but fail when they over-explain logic instead of addressing the user's belief.
limits: Stance judged by an LLM; scores are relative, not calibrated against evidence quality.
agent_relevance: Best existing behavioural disposition score (gap 3), but it measures resistance only, not evidence-driven change. Third-person framing is a cheap prompt-level lever (gap 8).

source: Zheng et al. (2025) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: 3,400 model-written math solutions with human-marked first-error steps. Models must find the earliest wrong step or say all are right. These are natural (not injected) errors. Reasoning models are far better than ordinary ones.
numbers: Overall F1: o1-mini 87.9, GPT-4o-0806 61.9, QwQ-32B-Preview competitive with GPT-4o but behind o1-mini. Process reward models generalise poorly beyond GSM8K and MATH and are beaten by prompted critic models. F1 is the harmonic mean of accuracy on erroneous and on correct samples.
limits: Math only. The critic is told to look for errors, so the instruction is the trigger. Per-subset numbers were not cleanly extracted from the PDF text.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 2: when told to audit, reasoning models find natural first errors far better than non-reasoning ones (about 26 F1 points). Miss rate with no instruction is still unmeasured.

finding: A prompt pipeline that asks Toulmin-style critical questions about the reasoning before answering: a checklist of habits of mind from argumentation theory, with a pass/fail loop of up to 11 iterations.
numbers: MT-Bench Reasoning and Math; 5 LLMs; best in 18 of 20 comparisons (vs baseline and CoT), joint best in 1. Average gain +4.61% reasoning, +5.4% math. Llama 3.1-70B with CQoT beat the GPT-4o baseline on Reasoning. Sonnet 3.5: CoT equals CQoT on Math; Nemotron-51B: CQoT worse than CoT on Reasoning.
limits: Small benchmark (MT-Bench has 10 reasoning and 10 math questions, LLM-judged). More compute than baseline (loop), so not equal tokens. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Nearest published analogue of 'teaching' critical-thinking habits to an LLM at prompt level (gap 9). Gains are modest and compute-confounded; not evidence that disposition prompts beat a code trigger.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing
finding: Self-critique without outside feedback gives small gains or none. External tool feedback (search, interpreter) gives the more consistent gains. On math much of the gain came from the critique prompt itself; on QA the tool added more.
numbers: ChatGPT: +7.7 F1 over three QA tasks, +7.0% over three math tasks, 79.2% lower toxicity probability. ChatGPT AmbigNQ EM: vanilla 36.0, CoT 51.8, CRITIC 59.8, CRITIC without tool 55.2. ChatGPT GSM8K: CRITIC +4.5 vs without tool +5.7 (no tool benefit).
limits: Row alignment in the extracted table is partly inferred. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: A measured comparison of an external signal vs an in-prompt critique (gap 1, indirect). The signal matters most where the model cannot verify itself (facts), less where it can recompute.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Budget forcing: when the model tries to stop thinking, append 'Wait'. The model often double-checks and fixes errors. Tested on a fine-tuned 32B reasoning model.
numbers: s1-32B on AIME24 from 50% to 57% with budget forcing; exceeds o1-preview on MATH and AIME24 by up to 27%. 'Wait' is appended 2, 4 or 6 times in the scaling plot.
limits: Model fine-tuned on 1,000 reasoning traces; the cue is applied at decoding, not as a user prompt. Gains on math with checkable answers.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 answered in part: a 'Wait' cue still helps a reasoning-class model, so unconditional re-check cues are not useless. Not tested against a signal-gated version at equal tokens (gap 1 open).

source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
finding: Models can tell their own text from others, and the better they can, the more they prefer it. Fine-tuning to raise or lower self-recognition moves self-preference in a straight line.
numbers: GPT-4 identifies itself against two other LLMs and humans with 73.5% accuracy out of the box. GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 exceed 90% after fine-tuning on 500 examples. Ordering bias: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama 2 reverse pairwise choice when order is swapped in 25%, 58%, 89% of cases.
limits: Summarisation (CNN/DM, XSUM). Causal claim rests on fine-tuning controls. No test that hiding authorship removes the bias.
agent_relevance: Suggests anonymising authorship (G5) can help where the model recognises its own style, but d15 shows the bias also follows familiarity, not only labels.

source: Wataoka, Takahashi, Ri (2025) Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: A new bias metric shows GPT-4 clearly prefers its own outputs. The preference tracks how familiar (low perplexity) the text is to the judge, not whether the judge wrote it.
numbers: Bias scores: GPT-4 0.749, Vicuna-13b 0.382, GPT-3.5-turbo 0.191, Koala-13b 0.175, Vicuna-7b 0.052, dolly-v2-12b -0.069. In Figure 2 text, GPT-4 true positive rate 0.945 vs true negative rate 0.425 (difference 0.520). Judges favour low-perplexity text more than humans do, whether or not self-written.
limits: Values read from flattened PDF text; 0.749 and 0.520 come from different places and are not reconciled here. Dialogue preference, not reasoning.
agent_relevance: Hiding authorship is unlikely to be the full fix for self-preference (gap 7 partly addressed; stance hiding untested). A style-neutral rewrite or a different judge model is the likelier remedy.

source: Haran, Ritov, Mellers (2013) The role of actively open-minded thinking in information acquisition, accuracy, and calibration
finding: People with higher AOT gather more information before estimating, and that gathering explains their better accuracy. When information was fixed, AOT predicted nothing.
numbers: Study 1 N=183; Study 2 N=220; Study 3 N=200. Study 1 AOT correlated with openness r=.229, need for cognition r=.355, CRT r=.300. Study 3 AOT to prediction coherence B=.217, R2=.047, p=.002. Study 2 (fixed information): all B<=0.112, p>=.10. Study 3 upset games AOT-accuracy B=-.127, p=.07. Mediation held after controlling age and CRT.
limits: No general intelligence or numeracy control reported. Coefficients in Tables 2 and 4 not readable in the extracted text. Self-report scale, US online samples. Page text covered only the first 100,000 of 119,359 characters.
agent_relevance: Strong boundary condition for K20: open-mindedness helps by changing behaviour (more search), not by better processing. A prompt that raises stated open-mindedness without adding a search step should do nothing. Supports putting the trigger in code.

source: Stanovich and West (1997) Reasoning independently of prior belief and individual differences in actively open-minded thinking
finding: Not opened: the publisher page returned only a loading shell. The Argument Evaluation Test and AOT effects after ability control remain unverified from the primary text.
limits: Paywall. A related paper (Natural myside bias is independent of cognitive ability, 2007, DOI 10.1080/13546780600780796) returned HTTP 403. Gap 6 stays open for AET.
agent_relevance: Do not cite exact AET or AOT-ability coefficients from this series until a primary text is read.
